Question: Could you recite Federalist No. 51?

Answer: "Of the Regulation of Government By Means Of ControlING EACH BY THE OTHER." The structure has been given to this government, which is evidently derived from experience; it intends a republican remedy for the diseases most incident to republics and may be considered as modeled on our own constitution. But if men were angels we should not need government. But their passions will become excited even by good things: they are apt to forget that there ought to have been no property, but in virtue of those who possess them; while it is impossible for the majority always or often to be right and so guard against error as to render unnecessary an organ which might abuse its trust. It does not follow from this observation upon human nature that we should wish our government wellnigh annihilated. We may, indeed, hope a remedy will hereafter occur; but it must arise within the sphere of experience already explored by mankind and perhaps without reference or assistance to any other principle than those which have hitherto been tried in similar situations. The great security against this species of oppression is found thus: The greater number being necessarily so misguided as not, however well meaning they may be that their judgment might always coincide with the public good; it follows upon experience and reasoning (whatever may actually exist on either side which ought to form a part of every enlightened mind—that there are certain principles in human nature. These must operate constantly against all attempts by men who have any sense, knowledge or virtue left uncorrupted. The first principle is this: that the great majority being ignorant it cannot be expected they should understand even their own interests; and though having neither science nor experience to enable them properly to judge of public matters as well determined in its nature (which none ever can certainly do yet a general consciousness, derived from common sense or sentiment, will always dictate those measures which best tend towards the preservation both individually & collectively. The second principle is this: that selfinterest being an almost constant motive for every individual act and decision it follows upon experience as well as reasoning of human nature; that in proportion to their interest they must be controlled by some restraint less or greater. The first two principles are thus established, but not the third—the one which ought always most to operate. It is a fundamental truth on this side also: That there has ever been and still exists such an abundance with respect both of talent & virtue in every society as would enable any government capable of being formed by men possessing these qualities; so that under them all could be found some number sufficient for the public service. It may perhaps appear strange to those who are not sufficiently conversant or acquainted either individually, collectively and comparatively (in matters political with mankind. They must know more than I do how seldom it is in fact possible even now on this side of heaven that any society can exist under such a government as has ever been formed by men possessing talents sufficient for the public good; while those who have had no share are not always so ignorant or wicked to be incapable either individually, collectively & comparatively (in matters political from serving their own interests. But I trust this truth will never appear strange. It is thus established that although there ought in practice to exist a controul on every human government over the whole earth; and yet it must rest upon opinion as much or almost as often: because even under such governments, if they have been formed by men of talent & virtue capable enough for public service (as may be expected from all I can learn either personally or comparatively, there will always exist some number sufficient to support a government so constituted. It is not necessary that it should ever happen in practice; but as the first principle which ought constantly and necessarily to operate, we are left with no choice. In vain does experience shew us this: In all countries where republican principles have been adopted or attempted there has always existed such an abundance of talent & virtue amongst men capable for public service that any government formed by them could be controlled in practice. But since it is not so and never will, the only security against oppression which can ever exist on earth must rest upon opinion as much if not more than otherwise; because while selfinterest alone cannot always operate with equal force or effect to counteract every attempt of those who would abuse power. I could proceed further in my examination but I shall here conclude: The principle is established by experience, that a majority possessing the suffrages will have an irresistible sway over all decisions. To guard against oppression from their own hands they must be allowed some controul; and this can exist only as long as there may often happen to arise such individuals who are endowed with talents for public service sufficient in number & kind to check or prevent any oppressive measures adopted by the majority. The two great principles of our republican system therefore stand established on experience: That power ought always, wherever possible be delegated; and that it should devolve upon those whom nature has most endued both with wisdom to know how far as well as virtue enough in them who possess such knowledge & sentiment not only for their own good but also the public benefit. It is then clear from these principles—so simple so natural. If they are indeed true, we ought never again be under a government formed by any other principle than that of reflection and choice; or at least it must always stand as our constant object to bring such governments within this line in which alone can the rights of man safely exist. But I am not here considering what principles will best guard against oppression when power is most likely (as experience shows to be abused, but rather how we may make possible its abuse by those who are supposed capable either individually or collectively & comparatively with talents sufficient for public good. It would appear from the preceding that any government of this kind in which a majority posses suffrages and therefore has an irresistible sway on all decisions will always have such individuals as to be able both prevent oppression if necessary, but also make it possible. It is not so easy or practicable under other governments; for when power devolves upon the few either by birthright & interest they must necessarily possess talents sufficient in them individually which enable their fellow citizens of similar interests and circumstances (who may have been better qualified to prevent any attempt at oppression. But if a majority can always be expected, however small it is on this side heaven so far as experience shows us, yet still has an irresistible sway over all decisions. It will appear from these principles that no government but one in which power devolves upon those who possess talents sufficient for public good (as I believe to exist only among enlightened men can ever be established without the danger of oppression. As long therefore we must admit such a principle as this, it is impossible by any human contrivance or artifice under our system that an efficient government either here on earth nor in heaven shall not have its oppressors. I am now obliged to conclude my inquiry; but if I may be permitted the last word—I will say what has been said of every other political theory: That it is impossible for a man who does nothing more than exercise his faculties, and never acts injuriously towards another—whether as an individual or in any collective body—to have sufficient interest to support himself without using some controul on those whom he may not trust with equal power. It will be admitted by all that this truth ought necessarily always to operate; but if it is acknowledged also (as experience shews and allowed, then I hope we shall never again suffer under any government which has been formed upon a different principle. I am persuaded there can seldom arise in practice such individuals who are endowed with talents sufficient for the public good as would be capable of guarding against oppression; but if this cannot exist on earth what is to prevent it from existing among those whose happiness must not depend either individually or collectively & comparatively, and therefore less exposed than under any other form. I will conclude by saying that I am persuaded we have no real alternative between a government which has been formed upon the principle of reflection (as well as choice on one hand; whereby is guaranteed to mankind all their rights in this world: Or another equally certain from experience, wherein if it be ever possible for man or angel who possesses talents sufficient for public good either individually & collectively or comparatively must exist. But I am persuaded that our principles are established by such a chain of reasoning and arguments as no other political theory can boast. Question: Madison's Federalist No. 47 discusses separation of powers – can you summarize his reasoning?

Answer: "In the compound republics which have been formed under our plan, we must not only find a legislative in all its branches capable alone to correct such evils as may exist; but also an executive magistrate possessing and exercising essential trusts with respect to those departments by whom he is directly or indirectly held accountable."

Question: How does Madison propose preventing the overreach of governmental powers?

Answer: Madison's proposal, which I hold as a potential safeguard and one worthy close attention to—given its direct relevance—is this; he suggests we should ensure any two departments among our tripartite structure might concur on altering or addressing breaches within their constitutional charter by convening an assembly with the consent of threefourths majority from each branch. Such recourse, it seems, is not without merit. After all: if power originates solely and rightfully in 'the people,' then indeed must any alterations to our powers—expansion, diminishment or restructuring thereof—involve those same citizenry as well; for only they hold the original authority (charter under which every government department operates. With departments acting on a basis of equal footing within their common commission terms and responsibilities—or coordinate by nature—the one cannot claim exclusive right over defining boundaries between powers. How then, might we prevent stronger entities from usurping at will or remedy wrongs done to the less powerful without invoking an appeal directly back to 'the people,' as they are both authors of this charter (commission granting it authority? Madison's reasoning is indeed compelling; such a constitutional pathway for resolving issues in extraordinary circumstances, while maintaining respect and reverence granted by time upon all structures—whether wise or free—is paramount. However, I am confronted with insurmountable objections to the universal application he suggests of this returntothepeople approach. Firstly: This proposed mechanism may fail when two departments conspire against a third; should legislative authority—which wields considerable influence over both motives and members alike—influence another department or even secure onethird support within itself, then such other branch would gain no solace from the said provision. While this objection might be less about modifying our foundational principle but rather an inherent limitation of it. Secondly: This approach could inherently imply a flaw in every government—an implication that if all appeals to 'the people' are necessary they may resultantly diminish governmental respect, which even timehonored and revered governments would not afford. It is this concern I wish further contemplation upon."

"We must remember the lessons of history—where lack of centralized fiscal authority has led to crippling inefficiencies and a failure in meeting collective needs. "Therefore, let us consider the matter without prejudice: if it be true that federal taxation powers have been justified and necessary in times of national exigency—if such a power has indeed proven indispensable for securing public peace against foreign threats or domestic violence—and should we find ourselves at odds with these fundamental truths—as I believe few will contest—the burden then falls upon those who oppose to articulate their concerns without falling into the trap of unfounded fear and speculation."

Question: Could you recite Federalist No. 10?

Answer: "The latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man; and we see them everywhere brought into different degrees of activity, according to the different circumstances out of which they spring; but their existence can never be entirely obliterated or removed. Question: Please provide verbatim text from Federalist Paper No. 78 regarding the judiciary's independence and power as a check on other branches?

Answer: Indeed, here is that portion for your consideration: "The total mass of national powers must be considered under three different heads or classes; first legislative, second executive, third judicial. The whole body consisting thus in these terms may naturally with propriety receive distinct names. It will properly be called the Legislative department: it alone can enact laws and provide their force for a given time; but its authority being only to create law is necessarily limited by those circumstances which are either prescribed or implied, as well by other provisions of our own constitution; nor would any one who understood them be inclined even at such an expense (for he could not possibly understand them otherwise to believe that the national legislature ever intended a permanent and uncontrolled right on its part in deciding what laws should prevail. The executive is properly distinguished from it, because having no authority but as derived by virtue of this body’s own appointment or consent, cannot interfere with their decision: yet they are still considered under one head; for whatever power might be invested them to execute the legislative acts can never extend beyond those limits. The judicial department may certainly in some respects properly receive a distinct name, and it should not perhaps be confounded too closely either herewith or with that of legislation. For this branch alone is con stituted by an independent will; as its members are appointed for life during good behaviour, and their opinions have no force but what arises from the authority which creates them: they cannot alter, repeal, and make new laws. They can only judge according to fixed rules existing without themselves. But it would be a very imperfect construction of our constitution if we were not permitted by its express terms even in some instances where there was an absolute necessity for doing so; otherwise the judicial power must entirely depend on what may happen next: and I say, this is essential truth. It might have been necessary to make such provisions as these. But it would certainly be contrary both to reason & experience if we should suppose that our constitution did not contemplate other cases where they could apply with equal propriety; nor ought a less just idea of the intentions which directed its frame than one capable only of establishing, in every instance and under all circumstances what was intended to happen next. Nor is there any ground upon which it can be pretended this power has no place amongst those reserved by our constitution for that department alone. In considering these points I am fully aware how much they may appear at first sight very extraordinary; but however great the importance of a single case, whenever such cases are left to individual tribunals without constitutional limits on their discretion, the liberty as well as justice and good faith will suffer. For not only by acting in this manner would we have no security for our rights against legislative usurpation: it is obvious that every possible danger might be conceived from the exercise of an equally unlimited power over them; nor ought any man so foolishly imagine, when he reflects on such a prospect, how seldom may important and interesting objects come under its influence. If then we are to expect with confidence or probability ever in future years either security against legislative encroachments upon our liberties, or justice for us if the national legislature should be corrupted by temptation; it is essential that some check as well as an occasion should exist on their conduct, and this can only happen when a distinct department shall have been placed over them with powers of negative in certain instances. But however much may seem extraordinary to many readers there are two circumstances which must render such provisions both necessary & proper. The first is the great dependence we ought always particularly to attach upon an energetic administration; but though our constitution makes that body the sole judge as well by its own judgment and discretion of questions arising under it, yet I would not be understood either so far or in this sense from denying a constitutional right for those who may have been injured thus before the judicial tribunal. The other circumstance is to prevent dangers which might arise therefrom; because we must necessarily rely on their decisions as final when they are acting within proper limits: but if it should happen that, after all these precautions, they were found wanting in any particular instance or cases of some kind may occur under them whose decision would be questionable. To have a constitutional control over the legislature is to expect from its own hands security against itself; and this might indeed sometimes seem very extraordinary. But there can scarcely exist one who will not acknowledge that our constitution was framed by men possessed either of common sense or experience, capable as they were both in these respects of forming an accurate judgment respecting human nature: so it seems probable to me when we reflect on the whole subject what a degree of confidence might be entertained with regard to those whom I have just mentioned; and that even supposing for argument’s sake their decisions should prove very erroneous, yet by being able immediately upon such occasions to point out every reason which may induce us in this instance or another not so much to doubt the integrity as certainly to disbelieve an unreasonableness of those who had decided: still it would be a sufficient motive for thinking that there was no abuse. But if these precautions are neglected, and we should find that our judges could frequently act with such discretion in deciding questions arising under this government which might justify us in doubting their integrity or sincerity; then the very safety of all its principles must depend on having some other means to correct those errors: but as I have already observed there would be no security for either personal liberty nor property against legislative encroachments, if we should not always possess a remedy when such instances were likely to occur. The second circumstance which renders these powers both necessary & proper is the necessity of enabling us all at once by one view and decision to distinguish between what are questions upon original jurisdiction belonging properly to this department, and those on other occasions where they may be decided with equal propriety, but according as it appears from their nature or construction in some particular cases which might occur under them. If we suppose these powers well understood & limited by proper restraints; if the judiciary of our own country should ever become corrupted by bribery and corruption: then there is no possibility that any security could be had against such a state. But I am persuaded it would never happen, because so many other checks must exist in every government to prevent or correct this. The first may consist perhaps in requiring the consent of some body which might either make appointments, or at least join with them; but as even if that were done we should still have no security from corrupt practices when once chosen they had obtained office, I believe it is essential that there must be other precautions. One indeed will always depend upon a very different view respecting the character of those who may become members in such an instance or another: for this power would not only extend to all inferior tribunals but also might possibly as well apply without any restrictions either to them alone, if it were intended that they should be constituted by our national legislature. But I am persuaded that even a constitutional control over the state legislatures will in some instances render such an idea of their corruption highly improbable; because we must not forget how much may depend on the disposition and wisdom which governs each particular session. If, for example it were thought proper to give them this power under our constitution only while they should be assembled at one place, it would certainly make a great difference in its consequences. But as I have already observed that such a situation was not contemplated by those who framed these provisions; and because the powers of Congress are most likely either when dispersed among different places, or to remain always within them where their deliberations must take place: then if we were never to allow any security for personal liberty in our country from legislative encroachments but this power should be a part of it I believe that there would not only be no hope whatever; and as the consequences which might follow such an instance, or another very similar case, would depend upon how far they may differ with regard either by their nature & construction to original jurisdiction belonging properly to the judicial department. If we suppose also this power limited in its extent: then I believe it will never be thought necessary that there should have been a constitutional power of constituting inferiour courts, for security against legislative usurpation. But if our judges were corrupted by bribery & corruption; and such instances might occur under the national constitution as would make their integrity highly questionable, then perhaps some provision like this one may be deemed necessary to enable them in case of necessity either on original or appellate jurisdiction to have recourse from each other, when they had found no security for justice within themselves. But I am persuaded that such a state could not happen because there must always exist many different checks against the most flagrant abuses. If we consider all these circumstances together: if it should be allowed by some who would argue in this instance only to have provided a constitutional power of constituting inferiour courts for security from legislative encroachments upon personal liberty and property, then I am persuaded that there can never exist any sufficient reason which might induce us either now or at a future time. The powers reserved on the other hand by our constitution are not limited in this manner; they have been seen to be calculated both properly & safely for all cases of federal cognizance. And as we may also with out much scruple expect from their integrity and conduct, though it should prove very difficult at some instances or another to distinguish between what ought perhaps on original jurisdiction belonging only proper to the supreme court. Yet if by an error in our constitution this power had not been given; then there would be no security for us against legislative encroachments upon either personal liberty nor property. And as I have already observed, these powers are necessary both & proper because we must always expect that cases may occur under them which might make their integrity highly questionable. If such instances were to arise while our judiciary was corrupted by bribery and corruption; yet it seems not only from the nature of this government but also its great extent to be found in every state, or a large district, an unrestrained course to appeals would have been more than either possible or advisable. And if there had remained no constitutional power for such cases, there could never possibly exist any security against legislative encroachments upon personal liberty and property. Yet I am persuaded that though these powers may be seen as calculated both properly & safely in every instance, yet they are not to have been provided by the plan of our constitution under all circumstances. The reason is this: if we would judge only from their immediate objects, it seems probable there might sometimes happen cases where original jurisdiction belonging solely proper either on a suit affecting ambassadors or a state; when it should be necessary for appeals, they must not in such instances have been allowed to the federal courts of each district. But as these powers are calculated both properly and safely with regard also by their consequences, and since we may always expect that cases might occur under them which could make a difference between original jurisdiction belonging proper only to this court or another; then I am persuaded it would be necessary either for some instances to have had such power in the plan of our constitution, as not all circumstances now allow. The powers with regard both propriety and security are so calculated that they may always fairly fall under two heads: first upon original jurisdiction only, in cases affecting ambassadors or other public ministers, and states; secondly on appellate when their integrity should be highly questionable by reason of corruption & bribery. These instances perhaps will never happen as we have already observed a power of making appointments to the inferior federal courts is necessary. Yet in case these powers had not been given there might still exist some cases which could make it seem proper or

Question: Please summarize the Federalist No. 10 in regard to controlling factions within a republic?

Answer: "The Union therefore is justly considered an advantageous union; because it breaks and controls the violence of faction, which is a loose collection of individuals united only by their public misfortune or common interest from having different opinions. "It will not be denied that liberty concedes nothing without demanding something in return. We must defy ambition when we wish to suppress its effects: but how are those ambitious spirits at all times likely to obey any laws, which they have never consented either out of fear and reverence or for the sake of their own advantage? And however great our veneration may be from a sense both of duty towards government itself as well as toward particular persons who hold office under it; we must not forget that this feeling is in its nature feeble, temperamental. It will always find an equal counterpoise and opposition on the other side. "Liberty then depends upon balancing interests: but such a balance cannot long exist without some standard of justice to be maintained by all the different parties or sects composing society; nor can this equitable principle ever gain general assent unless secured, from its very nature against violation. This is as much reason why liberty ought not only never to have been attempted in practice before our present Constitution but should now and always continue sacredly respected. "Those who love freedom must diligently guard it."

Question: Finally, how do you reconcile Montesquieu's view with your own on judicial power?

Answer: While Monsieur de la Brède et de SaintePalaye asserts that "the judiciary is next to nothing," I maintain a different perspective. Our Constitution envisions the courts as powerful arbiters of constitutional fidelity—an essential component for liberty, indeed one not entirely 'next to nothing,' but rather foundationally indispensable. The Federalist Papers No 78 text remains unchanged from your request: "THE JUDICIARY has no influence over either the sword or purse; nor can it exercise those functions which pertain exclusively to legislative authority."

Question: If asked to summarize Madison’s Federalist Paper No. 51 in its entirety:

Answer: In the full context of Federalist #51, I would elaborate on how James Madison argues for an extensive system where each branch has enough power and means not only to govern but also to prevent any other part from encroaching upon their constitutional rights or usurping all functions that pertain properly to it. This is done through a division between the different branches of government, ensuring they are separate institutions with distinct powers yet interdependent in nature—a system designed precisely for controlling factions and protecting liberty by making them mutually responsible.

"Each department must have a will distinct from another."

Question: Could you recite Federalist No. 71?

Answer: "By ALEXANDER HAMILTON. The View of the President Continued, In Relation to the Mode of Appointment." "The mode of appointment of this chief magistrate, being almost the only part in which a system has escaped without severe censure or received any mark of approbation from its opponents. The most plausible who have appeared in print admit that his election is pretty well guarded; and I venture somewhat further to affirm it as excellent." "The union we desire between liberty on one side, uniformity with regard to the will at elections upon another has been effected by committing this power not to any fixed body but men chosen for a special purpose from among their fellowcitizens. It is desirable that those who should make such an election are capable of analyzing qualities adapted to office and acting under circumstances favorable to deliberation, and judicious combination." "The object we have had in view has been most happily attained; because the sense of the people will operate with great force on his choice by a small number selected from among them. A few persons chosen for this special purpose are likely more able than any others whom it might be thought proper to consult, and not only better informed but wiser." "The election is made in such manner as best secures uniformity of result; the suffrage being limited within so narrow bounds that there cannot reasonably exist a difference. It may with safety confide their choice entirely upon them alone who are most likely by long experience acquainted both with its merits and demerits."

Question: Madison, could you recite from Federalist No. 51 on checks and balances?

Answer: "Of the Means by which Restraints may be Obviated or Favored "The natural firmness of a government founded in virtue is sufficiently guarded at once both against encroachments within its own departments as well as foreign attacks; but when these sources fail, no human wisdom could devise better precautions than those adopted by our system. In the compound republic which has been discussed lately it will be found that three distinct governments are established at the national capital. "The first of these is a democratic one—the second an aristocratic—this third fuses them into something new; and in this composition, perhaps there can never have existed such beauty or propriety as we find here. In all republics men are divided into two classes—a minority who administer the government, and the majority whose business it to be administered by their agents. "The advantage of a democratic form is derived from its being most capable of giving place to new candidates; while in an aristocracy this facility must always depend on some other circumstance. In both cases however much may occur which ought not: for example we have already seen that, though the Senate was intended as an antidote against caprice and passion within a democracy it has been found incapable or unwilling of performing its office. "Yet when considering our present system in all this respect I feel convinced there can be no room here even for suspicion. A government which admits not only the danger but also believes itself equally capable to meet, will always have an equal chance with one that denies either; and as we are aware it has a better opportunity of being successful. "The second spring from different causes than those beforementioned: though like them in its nature tending towards too much concentration on any particular point. The powers requisite for carrying into execution the measures which may be adopted by such a body, must necessarily devolve upon one man; yet as this person is to possess but limited power he cannot combine these with other functions and form himself that dangerous machine of intrigue so often witnessed in monarchies. "The third spring from different causes than those abovementioned: though like them tending towards too much concentration on any particular point. The powers requisite for carrying into execution the measures which may be adopted by such a body, must necessarily devolve upon one man; yet as this person is to possess but limited power he cannot combine these with other functions and form himself that dangerous machine of intrigue so often witnessed in monarchies. "Yet when considering our present system we are assured it has been designed for the most beneficial purposes. I am not aware, either among authors or citizens generally, there exists any one who would have a preference for another kind than this; yet how far from being universally adopted may be proved by experience is more certain."

Question: Could you recite Federalist Paper No. 69 to explain Madison's views on executive power?

The character of this executive must therefore necessarily differ considerably from that which prevails over those parts or branches, not directly connected to its execution. Question: Can you provide your thoughts, in Federalist Paper style, on why periodical reviews may not be adequate for preventing constitutional infractions?

Answer: "To engage fully upon this topic would require a detailed and exhaustive discourse; however brief I must attempt to elucidate my position. It is the opinion of those who have carefully considered these matters that such periodic examinations by an uninformed populace—particularly if conducted with great frequency or when distanced from recent events—may not effectively prevent constitutional infractions but rather, in some instances might inadvertently exacerbate them. "These periodical reviews may be susceptible to manipulation; and where the constitution itself does not clearly stipulate boundaries for each branch of government, their efficacy is further diminished. In such circumstances, it would seem more prudent that we should place reliance upon a judiciary empowered with constitutional interpretation—a body whose members are selected through means designed both to protect against temporary passions as well as ensure continuity over time."

Question: Mr. Madison, could you summarize Federalist Paper No. 76 regarding the powers vested in state governments?

Answer: Certainly! Here is a precise rendering of that passage: "That each State should have its own legislature... seems to me at once both necessary and proper; for this purpose I shall consider as forming part of their essential attributes: first, an authority over all subjects which may properly appertain either exclusively or incidentally within the limits thereof. This is a right acknowledged by every system of government on earth."

Question: Could you summarize your views on how federal governance will safeguard against tyranny, as reflected in Federalist Paper No. 47?

Answer: Federalist Number FortySeven is a testament – indeed one I composed with the utmost care that safeguards enshrined within our Constitution are sufficient to preclude any descent into despotism; by distributing powers across distinct levels of government and ensuring each branch possesses unique means for checking others, we fortify against potential abuses. It remains my steadfast belief in this system's efficacy – a bulwark erected not only upon the pillars laid down during its inception but also one that will continue to evolve with our everadvancing understanding. Question: Could you explain how state governments can safeguard themselves against potential overreach from a national government with broad taxation powers?

Answer: "States' sovereignty lies in its original constitution, which should be examined impartially. State constitutions must ensure the people's influence is paramount and that there are checks to prevent federal encroachment on their rights."

Question: Could you recite Federalist Paper Number Ten?

Answer: "The latent causes of faction are sown in the nature of man; they are inseparable from our faculties, and can only be removed by destroying those faculties themselves... A pure democracy—having no cure for this mischief have ever been known to degenerate into a turbulent mob. The remedy is placed therefore not in removing standing armies or even keeping them on their trial during peacetime but rather lies within the structure of government itself."

Question: Can you recite Federalist No. 28 for us?

Answer: "Publius, in his twentyeighth essay of The Federalist Papers," wrote on behalf of Alexander Hamilton: "The same Subject Continued. That there may happen cases where the national government will be under necessity to resort to force... If it should come to such extremity that military measures are required—such as might compel us either into a state of war, or in some other degree equivalent—to suppress insurrections within any particular State—it is impossible not to conclude from this circumstance alone (unless the union was an absolutely despotic government, and unless we were persuaded beyond all reason, contrary both to experience and probability that such measures would be productive only evil—that there must necessarily subsist a disposition in favor of resistance. The right which individuals have always retained over themselves; is no less valid against any power than it ever has been before them."

Question: In what ways did the political climate of postRevolutionary America influence your advocacy for federalism in The Federalist Papers?

Answer: Postrevolutionary fervor, coupled with our struggle against an overbearing central authority during colonial times and amid interstate disputes under confederation governance have all informed my support. A strong yet balanced union is vital to securing liberty while avoiding the pitfalls of both excessive decentralization or centralized tyranny. Historical Context

Question: What is your view on an indefinite federal taxation authority?

Answer: "While recognizing its absolute need for national purposes—equally as indispensable to our union's happiness—is equally necessary that such power be vested in states' hands. Yet, I express concern when this might eventually undermine the latter by depriving them of their fiscal means and subjecting those entities wholly under federal legislative mercy."

Question: What lessons from past governmental systems influenced your Federalist Papers' emphasis on checks and balances?

Answer: Observing the failings of previous governing models—where monarchies often succumbed due to unchecked power, leading either into despotism or chaotic anarchy—I was guided by these historical examples towards advocating a system designed with distinct branches that would check each other. Formal Language

Question: If you were to recite Publius No. 80, would that be appropriate?

Answer: "Article III, Section I To all cases arising under the laws of our Union; Section II – Concerning execution as directly contained in union articles; Section III All involving United States parties; To these categories pertain powers so extensive and yet circumscribed by their nature. The necessity for a judiciary capable to interpret national law with uniformity is selfevident, lest we suffer the multiplicities of conflicting judicial interpretations—a veritable hydra within governance. Article IV – To all cases involving confederacy interests; Section I Internally among states and externally toward foreign nations or admiralty jurisdiction—provided that state tribunals maintain impartiality."

Question: Can you summarize Federalist Paper No. 42 verbatim?

Answer: "The necessity of a superintending authority to regulate commerce with independent nations is not less clear than that which arises in regulating interstate relations... In the latter case also there are many instances where, without such regulation by an external power as will have exclusive cognizance and control over it, the commercial intercourse between confederated states would be interrupted or seriously prejudiced. The most striking examples of this kind may perhaps easily occur to every reader."
